etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English singen, from Old English singan, from Proto-West Germanic *singwan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ-. Cognate with German singen (“to sing”) and Danish synge (“to sing”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To produce musical or harmonious sounds with one’s voice.
(intransitive) To perform a vocal part in a musical composition, regardless of technique.
(transitive) To express audibly by means of a harmonious vocalization.

quote.citation: 1852, Mrs M.A. Thompson, “The Tutor's Daughter”, in Graham's American Monthly Magazine of Literature, Art, and Fashion‎[1], page 266:
quote.text: In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.

definitions.definition: (ornithology) To produce a 'song', for the purposes of defending a breeding territory or to attract a mate.
(literary) To produce any type of melodious vocalisation.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XXI, page 36:
quote.text: ⁠I do but sing because I must,And pipe but as the linnets sing:And unto one her note is gay,⁠For now her little ones have ranged;⁠And unto one her note is changed,Because her brood is stol’n away.

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 68:
quote.text: The evening was still very warm, and the birds in the woods were singing in praise of spring.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make a small, shrill sound.

quote.citation: 1715–1720, Homer, translated by Alexander Pope, “Book XXII”, in The Iliad of Homer, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:  […]  W[illiam] Bowyer, for Bernard Lintott […], →OCLC:
quote.text: O'er his head the flying spear / Sang innocent, and spent its force in air.

definitions.definition: To relate in verse; to celebrate in poetry.

quote.citation: 1718, Mat[thew] Prior, “Solomon on the Vanity of the World. A Poem in Three Books.”, in Poems on Several Occasions, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], and John Barber […], →OCLC, book II (Pleasure), page 468:
quote.text: Again I bid the mournful Goddeſs write / The fond Purſuit of fugitive Delight: / Bid her exalt her melancholy Wing, / And rais'd from Earth, and ſav'd from Paſſion, ſing / Of human Hope by croſs Event deſtroyed, / Of uſeleſs Wealth, and Greatneſs unenjoy'd,  […]

quote.citation: 1637, John Milton, “Lycidas”, in Poems of Mr. John Milton, […], London:  […]  Ruth Raworth for Humphrey Mosely, […], published 1646, →OCLC:
quote.text: Who would not sing for Lycidas? he knew Himself to sing, and build the lofty rhyme.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To display fine qualities; to stand out as excellent.

quote.citation: 2022 July 7, Sonia Fernandez, “‘Out of the Starting Gate’”, in The Current‎[2], University of California, Santa Barbara, archived from the original on 2022-07-07:
quote.text: [Alissa Monte said] “This result was all about demonstrating that LZ [the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment] works, and it does! As we take more data and mature our analyses, we get to make LZ sing.  […] ”

definitions.definition: (ergative) To be capable of being sung; to produce a certain effect by being sung.

quote.text: No song sings well unless it is open-vowelled, and has the rhythmic stress on the vowels. Tennyson's songs, for instance, are not generally adapted to music.

definitions.definition: (Australia) In traditional Aboriginal culture, to direct a supernatural influence on (a person or thing), usually malign; to curse. [from 19th c.]

quote.citation: 2002, Alex Miller, Journey to the Stone Country, Allen & Unwin, published 2003, page 343:
quote.text: ‘We sung them two real good. We never give Louis Beck no place to find rest from his torment.’

definitions.definition: The act, or event, of singing songs.

quote.citation: 1982, Douglas Adams, Life, the Universe and Everything, page 55:
quote.text: Then all three would go off in search of the first, give it a good talking to and maybe a bit of a sing as well.

quote.citation: 2002, Martha Mizell Puckett, Hoyle B. Puckett, Memories of a Georgia Teacher: Fifty Years in the Classroom, page 198:
quote.text: Some of the young folks asked Mrs. Long could they have a sing at her home that Sunday afternoon; she readily agreed, telling them to come early, bring their songbooks, and have a good sing.

quote.citation: 2016, Kerry Greenwood, Murder and Mendelssohn, Sydney: Allen and Unwin, page 287:
quote.text: 'Ah, yes, Miss Fisher, have you had a nice sing?'
